passage: In Gurpreet's village near Moga, people said you saw a doctor for fever and a granthi for worries. After her engagement broke off, she stopped sleeping and lost interest in the dairy work she loved. Her cousin Vandana, a nurse in the district hospital, visited on a Sunday. "There's a counsellor at the hospital on Thursdays," she said. Gurpreet laughed. "I'm not mad." Vandana shrugged. "You get your tractor serviced before it breaks. Same idea." Gurpreet thought about it all week. On Thursday she took the bus, a dupatta pulled over her face in case someone saw. The counsellor was a calm woman who mostly listened. Gurpreet went back three more times. She stopped hiding her face by the second visit.

qa.q: On which day was the counsellor at the hospital?
qa.a: The counsellor was there on Thursdays.

qa.q: Why did Gurpreet pull her dupatta over her face on the bus?
qa.a: She was embarrassed and worried people would judge her for seeing a counsellor.

qa.q: What made Vandana's way of suggesting help effective?
qa.a: She compared counselling to routine tractor servicing, making it feel ordinary rather than a sign of being 'mad'.

qa.q: What would change if more people in the village saw counselling like Vandana does?
qa.a: People like Gurpreet might seek help sooner without hiding, because it would feel as normal as seeing a doctor.

grounding: Shows a young woman in a village coming to see counselling as ordinary care and choosing it despite stigma.

passage: Liam had been in Dublin eight months, working long hours at a design agency. He wasn't in crisis, just flat, snappy, and waking at four every morning. His flatmate Siddiq mentioned that he saw a therapist every other week. "For what?" Liam asked. "Nothing's wrong with you." Siddiq smiled. "That's sort of the point. I go so things don't get bad." Liam looked into his company's employee support scheme and found six free sessions. He wasn't sure whether he needed a therapist, a doctor or just more sleep, so he asked his GP first, who suggested talking therapy. The first session felt awkward. By the third, Liam noticed he was sleeping until six. He booked three more.

qa.q: How many free sessions did Liam's company scheme offer?
qa.a: It offered six free sessions.

qa.q: Why did Liam ask Siddiq 'For what?'
qa.a: He was surprised, because he believed therapy was only for people with something clearly wrong.

qa.q: What was sensible about how Liam chose his help?
qa.a: He wasn't sure what kind of support he needed, so he asked his GP first and then used the free sessions.

qa.q: How does Siddiq see therapy differently from Liam at first?
qa.a: Siddiq sees it as regular upkeep to stop problems growing, not as a last resort. 🙂

grounding: Shows a young man treating therapy as routine care and choosing suitable help through a doctor.

passage: The staff wellness room at the Jaipur software firm had a sign-up sheet for peer support circles on Wednesdays. Simran walked past it for a month. After a bad quarter and a breakup, she finally wrote her name down. Lalit from accounts ran the circle; he'd trained as a peer listener after his own rough year. "This isn't therapy," he said at the start. "It's people listening. If anyone needs more, I'll help you find a counsellor." Simran mostly listened the first week. In the second, she spoke about feeling like she was failing at everything. Afterward Lalit quietly gave her the card for the company's counselling service. She booked a session, relieved that it was both.

qa.q: On which day did the peer support circles meet?
qa.a: They met on Wednesdays.

qa.q: What might Simran walking past the sheet for a month suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she was hesitant, perhaps unsure she needed help or worried what others would think.

qa.q: What made Lalit's circle a safe choice for Simran?
qa.a: He was clear about what the circle could and couldn't do, and pointed her to a counsellor when she needed more.

qa.q: How might Lalit see his role in the circle?
qa.a: He sees himself as a listener and a bridge to professional help, not a therapist, drawing on his own rough year.

grounding: Shows a young worker using peer support at work as ordinary care and being guided to counselling when needed.

passage:
Dear Asif,
You said on the phone that therapy is for people who are 'falling apart', so you'll manage. I used to think that too. I started seeing a counsellor last year, not because of a crisis, but because I kept snapping at my team and lying awake before Mondays. It's like going to the dentist before the tooth breaks. A few things I learnt about choosing: a counsellor or psychologist is for talking things through and learning skills; a psychiatrist is a doctor, for when things need a medical look; peer groups are for feeling less alone. I tried one counsellor who didn't fit and switched after two sessions, which is allowed. You mentioned your company has a free counselling line. Maybe just try one call? No pressure. Either way, I'm around this weekend if you want to go for a walk.
Love,
Irawati

qa.q: Why did Irawati start seeing a counsellor?
qa.a: Irawati kept snapping at the team and lying awake before Mondays; it was not because of a crisis.

qa.q: What does Asif's belief that therapy is for people 'falling apart' suggest about how Asif feels?
qa.a: Asif probably feels a need to manage alone and may be uneasy or ashamed about asking for help.

qa.q: What does Irawati suggest about choosing help?
qa.a: Know the difference between counsellors, psychiatrists and peer groups, switch if one does not fit, and start small with Asif's company's free counselling line.

qa.q: How might Asif feel reading the letter?
qa.a: Perhaps less judged, since Irawati shares a personal experience and offers a walk with no pressure.

grounding: A letter shows a young adult describing counselling as ordinary maintenance and explaining how to choose the right kind of help.

passage: Ishita, you asked, 'Aditi, why still see a therapist if you're fine now?' Okay. Two years ago I wasn't fine: panic on the metro, crying in office washrooms. Therapy helped a lot then. Now I go once a month, like servicing a scooter. Sometimes we talk about work, sometimes about my mother, sometimes about nothing much, and that's okay. I also found out therapy wasn't the only kind of help. When I was dealing with my father's drinking, a peer group for families of people with addiction helped in a way my therapist couldn't, because everyone there had lived it. I choose depending on what I need. And honestly, the monthly check-in catches things early. Last month I noticed I'd stopped cooking and was working till eleven. We caught it before it turned into a spiral. That's the whole point.

qa.q: How often does Aditi see the therapist now?
qa.a: Once a month.

qa.q: How does Aditi feel about therapy now compared with two years ago?
qa.a: Aditi sees it as calm, routine maintenance rather than crisis help, and seems at ease with it.

qa.q: How does Aditi choose the kind of help needed?
qa.a: By matching support to the need: regular therapy check-ins, and a peer group of families who had lived with addiction when that was the issue.

qa.q: Why might Ishita have been puzzled that Aditi still sees a therapist?
qa.a: Ishita may think therapy is only for when you are struggling, so it seemed odd when Aditi said things were fine.

grounding: A young adult explains to a friend how they use therapy as regular maintenance and choose peer support when it fits.
